newsitem.title: ITALY: Odds and ends from the food summit.
newsitem.headline: Odds and ends from the food summit.

text.p: The U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit brings together heads of state and government for a five-day gathering to discuss the global food situation.
The following is an assortment of observations and unexpected happenings at the summit being held at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) headquarters in Rome.
Want a lasting memento for a job well done at the food summit? FAO can produce just the thing. The organisation offers gold, silver and bronze commemorative medals for sale.
The bronze comes in at $30, the silver at $85 and the gold at $365 -- a dollar a day or exactly what the World Bank estimates to be the daily wage for 1.2 billion people.

World leaders are at the food summit and so is Christmas. For presidents and prime ministers with time on their hands and a yearning to celebrate, the FAO shop is the place to pick up party crackers and seasonal decorations.
They can even mail them home without running foul of Italy's notoriously unreliable postal system. The Dutch post office is offering a mail and parcel delivery service free to delegates.

The summit opened on Wednesday with approval of a declaration on food security that included formal recognition of the "fundamental contribution to food security by women...and the need to ensure equality between men and women."
Not long after, the Philippines' representative took to the podium, introduced to delegates by the English interpreter as "His Excellency Leticia Ramos-Shahani".
Ramos-Shahani, whi is mounting a campaign to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. Secretary General, is a woman.
If gender can be confusing, language is worse.

A speech by Israeli Agriculture and Environment Minister Rafael Eitan in Hebrew ground to a halt when the interpreter lost his way. The interpreter admitted he could not read Hebrew and was being led through an English translation.
"We are trying to find out exactly where the speaker is in the text that is in front of the interpreter," the startled leaders were told by way of a public apology.
Eitan had to start his speech again.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, confronted by stark figures, saw the naked truth at the summit.
Three women, protesting against genetically-engineered soybeans, hijacked his news conference by taking off all their clothes to reveal bare bodies painted with slogans
"I certainly earned my pay today," Glickman said, adding that it was "to say the least, one of the more interesting things that's ever happened to me in this job."
Security was stepped up at the summit after the "Gene Bean" striptease. But the long arm of the law unfortunately did not stretch as far as Marie-Therese Avemeka's hotel room.

Staff at her swish hotel on the Via Veneto asked Avemeka, Congo's minister for women's integration in development, to check her belongings after a small fire in her room. Police said she reported a watch and a gold bracelet had vanished.
Italian clothing company Benetton, well-known for controversial posters, have their name back on billboards across Rome in advertising associated with the summit.
But this time the firm that shocked with images of a black and white horse mating, bodies stamped "HIV positive" and a nun and a priest kissing, has raised no eyebrows.

The poster, also run as a newspaper advertisement in some European countries, features an empty wooden spoon on a white background. Benetton says it symbolises man's relationship with food -- or hunger.
